messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The event that fractured Carlos’s world happened three years ago, during a solo backcountry patrol in the national forest where he worked as a park ranger. He had been checking a remote trailhead when two men emerged from the tree line, demanding his truck and his radio. When he hesitated, they dragged him into the brush, bound his wrists with zip ties, and spent the next several hours beating him with a tire iron and a length of pipe. They broke three of his ribs, shattered his left kneecap, and fractured his orbital bone. He remembers the smell of pine needles and his own blood, the way the sky went from blue to orange to black, and then—nothing. The next thing he knew, he was waking up in a hospital bed three days later, his jaw wired shut. Some moments of that afternoon are excruciatingly clear: the sound of the first rib cracking, the metallic taste in his mouth. Others are complete blanks, like a film reel with whole sections cut out. When he tries to tell his therapist what happened, he loses the thread mid-sentence, his mind going white, and he cannot finish. He has come to believe that his brain is broken—that his reactions since the event mean he is going crazy, that his body has been permanently damaged in ways the doctors cannot see.

In the months that followed, Carlos returned to work on light duty, but the forest felt different. Every delay—a car that didn’t start, a colleague who was five minutes late to a meeting—sent a spike of adrenaline through him, his body reacting before his mind had time to think. He began checking the locks on his cabin door three, four, five times before bed, and then the windows, and then the deadbolt again. At work, he started rehearsing what he would say before any interaction with hikers or fellow rangers, running through possible conversations in his head because he was certain that if he said the wrong thing, it would trigger something dangerous. He could not rely on other people, he had decided; they were unpredictable, and unpredictability meant threat. The more he rehearsed, the more his memories of the assault felt fragmented and distant, as if he were watching himself from far away. He began numbing his feelings deliberately, pushing down any flicker of anger or fear because those emotions felt like the beginning of a spiral he could not control. His body, he was convinced, had been permanently weakened; the pain in his knee and the occasional double vision from the orbital fracture were proof that he was now vulnerable, a target.

The avoidance seeped into everything. He stopped driving altogether—both as a driver and as a passenger—because every car that slowed down or pulled alongside him at a stoplight made his chest tighten, and he would see the two men again, their faces blank and purposeful. He told his supervisor he preferred to patrol on foot, which limited his assignments and strained his relationship with the team. His colleagues began to notice that he seemed distant, that he would flinch when someone approached from behind, that he never joined them for after-work drinks. Carlos was aware of this, and it confirmed his belief that he could not rely on them anyway. The more he isolated himself, the more his memories of the assault surfaced unbidden—the partial clarity of certain moments, like the tire iron swinging down, and the blank gaps where his mind simply stopped. He would catch himself checking the door locks again, and the act of checking would trigger a flash of the zip ties biting into his wrists, which would make him feel even more convinced that his mind was unraveling.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a morning in late October when he could not bring himself to leave his cabin. He had spent two hours rehearsing a single phone call to his supervisor, then canceled it, then checked the door locks four times, then sat on the floor with his head in his hands, certain that something terrible was happening even though nothing had changed. He was tired of feeling like a stranger in his own life. He was afraid that if he did not get help, the gaps in his memory would grow, and he would lose the thread of himself entirely. What he wanted most was to stop feeling that his body was a broken thing, and to trust that the next car on the road was just a car.
